summary: Explains that the RFC Editor snapshots of Internet Official Protocol Standards, the xx00 documents, are replaced by a web page. Unpublished xx00 numbers up to 7000 are never issued, and from RFC 7100 they can be assigned.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7101 records the end of periodic RFC snapshots of the Internet standards list. The list is kept online, and unused RFC numbers ending in 00 can be assigned from RFC 7100 onward.

subtitle: Why RFC numbers ending in 00 are no longer reserved for standards lists.

tldr.problem: The RFC Editor once published periodic snapshots of Internet standards as RFCs ending in 00. An online list made those snapshots unnecessary.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7101 ends the snapshot series, moves STD 1 to Historic, and clarifies which unused round-number RFCs can be assigned.
tldr.outcome: The online list replaces the snapshots. Unissued numbers ending in 00 through RFC 7000 are marked never issued; from RFC 7100, such numbers are available for assignment.

today: RFC 7101 is an Informational document describing an administrative change. It ends the RFC snapshot series for the official standards list and frees qualifying RFC numbers for assignment.

sections.title: The History of the Standards Snapshots
sections.content: Starting with RFC 2200, RFC numbers ending in 00 were reserved for snapshots of the Internet Official Protocol Standards. The last snapshot was RFC 5000, published in May 2008. These documents listed Standards Track and Experimental documents.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs ending in 00 once held snapshots of the standards list. RFC 5000 was the last one.

sections.title: The Online List Replaces the Snapshots
sections.content: The RFC Editor had produced a dynamically updated online list since 2000. The IETF no longer saw a need to maintain periodic snapshots, so the official list would be provided online. RFC 7101 says the snapshot publication tradition is discontinued.
sections.plainLanguage: The standards list now lives online and can be updated there. The RFC Editor will no longer publish periodic snapshots.

sections.title: What Happens to the Reserved Numbers
sections.content: RFC 7101 directs the RFC Editor to mark unused numbers ending in 00 through RFC 7000 as never issued. From RFC 7100 upward, numbers ending in 00 are available for assignment to any RFC. The document also records that RFC 5000 and STD 1 move to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: Older unused round-number RFCs are marked never issued. From RFC 7100 onward, these numbers may be assigned to other RFCs.
